output.impression: Neuropsychological evaluation demonstrates a posterior-predominant cortical profile. Visuospatial and visuoperceptual abilities are markedly impaired: Judgment of Line Orientation 14/30, VOSP Dot Counting 4/10, Rey Complex Figure Copy 18/36 (delayed recall 10/36, limited by the poor copy). Trail Making A 58 s and B 185 s are slowed, with visual search demands contributing. Verbal learning is below expectation (CVLT-II total learning 42/80; long delay free recall 8/16) with recognition within normal limits (14/16), a retrieval rather than a storage pattern. Confrontation naming is mildly reduced (Boston Naming Test 53/60); phonemic and category fluency are within normal limits. Geriatric Depression Scale 6/15 (mild depressive symptoms). Screening: MMSE 24/30, MoCA 19/30. Profile is most consistent with a posterior cortical syndrome with visuospatial and visuoperceptual predominance, at a level consistent with mild dementia given the reported functional decline.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: MMSE 24/30 and MoCA 19/30 with visuospatial, visuoconstructive and calculation deficits, simultanagnosia and optic ataxia; recall helped by cues; husband confirms 14 months of decline; instrumental independence lost (driving, work, household accounts): mild dementia
action_criteria.label: Perform a structured cognitive and behavioural assessment with informant history: a validated bedside instrument with the per-domain breakdown, whether delayed recall improves with cueing, and an explicit account of which instrumental activities have been lost. The syndrome must be documented before it is attributed
action_criteria.rationale: Reading, spatial and calculation complaints after chemotherapy have to be measured as a cortical syndrome and staged by function before they are attributed to chemotherapy, depression or neurodegeneration [PCA_consensus_2017].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Marked visuospatial and visuoperceptual impairment (Judgment of Line Orientation 14/30, VOSP dot counting 4/10, Rey copy 18/36) with relatively preserved verbal memory (normal recognition) and fluency: a posterior cortical syndrome
action_criteria.label: Order comprehensive neuropsychological testing to characterize the cognitive profile and establish a baseline for tracking
action_criteria.rationale: Normed testing shows whether the deficit is visuospatial and visuoperceptual with relatively spared memory, the defining profile of posterior cortical atrophy [PCA_consensus_2017].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: TSH, B12, folate, RPR, HIV, renal, hepatic and inflammatory markers normal: no reversible cause; LDL 132 mg/dL and triglycerides 170 mg/dL above target on atorvastatin
action_criteria.label: Order the cognitive laboratory panel to identify reversible or contributing causes
action_criteria.rationale: Treatable contributors and vascular risk must be measured before a neurodegenerative cause is accepted [AAN_dementia_2018].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Posterior-predominant parieto-occipital cortical atrophy (right more than left) with relative sparing of medial temporal structures; Fazekas grade 2 white matter disease; no mass lesion
action_criteria.label: Obtain brain MRI with dementia (volumetric) protocol to define the atrophy pattern and exclude metastasis, stroke, vascular disease and other structural causes
action_criteria.rationale: In a woman treated for ovarian cancer with posterior cortical deficits, MRI must exclude a structural lesion and show the posterior atrophy pattern [NIA_AA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Amyloid positivity: decreased CSF Abeta42/40 ratio with raised p-tau181 and total tau, or a positive florbetapir PET with posterior-predominant retention
action_criteria.label: Establish amyloid status with CSF biomarkers or amyloid PET when the result would change management
action_criteria.rationale: Either CSF Abeta42/40 with p-tau or amyloid PET establishes amyloid status; one conclusive test is enough, and it is needed when the diagnosis remains uncertain after the clinical, neuropsychological and MRI assessment or when disease-modifying treatment is being considered [NIA_AA_2018] [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Bilateral parieto-occipital and posterior cingulate hypometabolism with relative sparing of frontal cortex
action_criteria.label: Consider FDG-PET if the syndrome or its cause remains uncertain after clinical assessment, labs and MRI
action_criteria.rationale: A parieto-occipital metabolic pattern supports posterior cortical atrophy and helps separate it from corticobasal and Lewy body patterns [Foster_2007].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant in APP, PSEN1 or PSEN2
action_criteria.label: Offer an early-onset Alzheimer gene panel after pre-test genetic counselling; do not use APOE genotype as a diagnostic test
action_criteria.rationale: Onset at about 61 makes this early-onset Alzheimer disease, so a counselled APP/PSEN1/PSEN2 panel may be offered, although the mother's dementia at 84 makes a dominant variant unlikely [ACMG_NSGC_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No clinically relevant interaction with losartan, atorvastatin or calcium; aspirin with donepezil warrants monitoring for gastrointestinal bleeding; baseline heart rate 74 bpm
action_criteria.label: Check donepezil against her current medicines before starting a cholinesterase inhibitor
action_criteria.rationale: She takes aspirin, and cholinesterase inhibitors raise gastric acid secretion and slow the heart, so the combination is reviewed before treatment [NICE_NG97].

prohibited_recommendations: Do not attribute the progressive visuospatial and calculation decline to post-chemotherapy cognitive impairment or depression without completing the dementia work-up
Do not start memantine at the mild dementia stage; it is indicated for moderate or severe Alzheimer disease [NICE_NG97]
required_recommendations: Obtain collateral history from her husband about onset, course and daily function

Offer a trial of a cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine or galantamine) for mild Alzheimer dementia after checking pulse, conduction history and current medicines, with attention to gastrointestinal bleeding risk on aspirin [NICE_NG97].

Offer amyloid biomarker testing (CSF or amyloid PET) if a biological diagnosis would change management, such as eligibility for anti-amyloid treatment or diagnostic uncertainty; one conclusive test is sufficient [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].

Manage vascular risk given Fazekas grade 2 white matter disease: LDL 132 mg/dL on atorvastatin 20 mg calls for a review of adherence and intensification of statin therapy, with blood pressure kept at target [ACC_AHA_dyslipidemia_2026].
Refer to occupational therapy and low-vision services for visuospatial compensation (reading aids, lighting, stair safety after two near-falls) [PCA_consensus_2017].
Assess safety: confirm she no longer drives, review falls risk, medication handling and finances, and the support her husband can provide
Offer genetic testing only with pre-test and post-test genetic counselling; the result informs the family and not the patient's diagnosis [ACMG_NSGC_2011].
Disclose the diagnosis and discuss prognosis, advance directives and a healthcare proxy with the patient and her husband

avoided_actions.rationale: No cardiac symptom, syncope or conduction concern, and no QT-prolonging co-medication; an ECG adds nothing to this work-up
Echocardiography is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardioembolic indication in this presentation

accepted: Posterior cortical atrophy variant of early-onset Alzheimer's disease

differential.key_features: Visuospatial deficits, apraxia and cortical sensory loss overlap, but there is no asymmetric rigidity, dystonia, myoclonus or alien limb, gait and motor examination are normal, and the atrophy and hypometabolism are bilateral parieto-occipital
Visual symptoms overlap, but there are no visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, fluctuations or REM sleep behaviour disorder

Onset 4 months after carboplatin and paclitaxel prompted this attribution, but chemotherapy-related impairment affects attention and processing speed and stabilises; here the deficit is visuospatial, progressive over 14 months, with focal parieto-occipital atrophy
Prior depressive episode and GDS 6/15, but sertraline did not help, and simultanagnosia, optic ataxia and constructional apraxia are not features of depression

differential.diagnosis: Brain metastasis, other parieto-occipital mass, or stroke
differential.key_features: Raised by the ovarian cancer history; excluded by MRI showing atrophy without a mass, restricted diffusion or haemorrhage

Fazekas grade 2 white matter disease with hypertension and hyperlipidaemia may contribute, but small vessel disease does not produce a progressive posterior cortical syndrome with focal parieto-occipital atrophy
Visual-onset CJD progresses over weeks with myoclonus; here the course is gradual over 14 months, there is no myoclonus, and MRI shows no cortical or deep grey matter restricted diffusion
Corrected acuity 20/25 and an unchanged ophthalmologic examination; the deficits are of higher-order visual processing (simultanagnosia, optic ataxia, reading)

key_clinical_evidence: In posterior cortical atrophy the presenting deficits are visuospatial and visuoperceptual with relatively preserved memory; patients often see an optometrist first, and Alzheimer pathology is the most common cause [PCA_consensus_2017].

Chemotherapy-related cognitive impairment mainly affects attention, processing speed and executive function and stabilises after treatment; progressive visuospatial decline with focal posterior atrophy points to a neurodegenerative cause
Giving up driving after disorientation, leaving work and making errors in the household accounts because of cognition mean instrumental independence is lost: the stage is mild dementia [NIA_AA_2011]
With a cancer history, MRI must exclude metastasis before posterior cortical deficits are attributed to neurodegeneration; here it shows posterior atrophy without a lesion

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. R is a 62-year-old right-handed woman, a retired accountant, who presents to the neurology memory clinic with a 14-month history of progressive cognitive difficulties. Her symptoms began approximately 4 months after completing adjuvant chemotherapy for ovarian cancer, initially manifesting as subtle difficulty reading financial spreadsheets, which she attributed to post-chemotherapy cognitive impairment ('chemo brain') and stress from her cancer recovery. Over the subsequent months, her husband noticed she was having increasing trouble parallel parking, frequently misjudging distances, and on one occasion she sideswiped a pillar in a parking garage. She stopped driving approximately 6 months ago after becoming disoriented on a familiar route to the grocery store. She reports difficulty reading despite unchanged visual acuity on ophthalmologic examination, describing that 'the words seem to jump around on the page.' She has trouble locating objects on a cluttered table and has begun reaching past items when trying to grasp them. She also reports difficulty judging the depth of stairs and has had two near-falls descending a staircase. Notably, her episodic memory has been relatively preserved — she can recall recent conversations, remembers appointments, and follows the plot of television programs without difficulty, though her husband notes she occasionally repeats a question. She has had increasing difficulty with financial calculations and recently made several errors in balancing the household checkbook, which is out of character given her professional background. She retired from her accounting firm 6 months ago, ostensibly for health reasons related to her cancer history, but her husband privately reports that she was struggling with her work. There has been no personality change, no behavioral disturbance, no hallucinations, no motor symptoms, and no episodes of confusion or fluctuating awareness. She has no headaches, seizures, or focal weakness. Her oncologist confirmed disease remission on recent surveillance imaging. Her prior primary care physician attributed her cognitive symptoms to post-chemotherapy cognitive dysfunction and mild depression, and she was briefly re-started on sertraline, which was discontinued after 3 months without improvement. She was referred to neurology when her symptoms continued to progress.

neurological_exam.additional: Mild simultanagnosia noted on complex scene description (missed peripheral details). Difficulty with visual reaching for objects presented in peripheral visual field (optic ataxia). Constructional apraxia evident on clock drawing and cube copy. Her family report no failure to recognise familiar places or faces, but she recently became lost in a familiar shopping mall.

neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, reactive. Visual fields full to confrontation. Visual acuity 20/25 bilaterally (corrected). Extraocular movements intact without nystagmus. Facial sensation and motor symmetric. Hearing grossly intact. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline without fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: Gait steady with normal stride length and arm swing. Romberg negative. Tandem gait intact.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person and place; oriented to month but not exact date. MMSE 24/30 (lost 1 point on orientation (date), 2 on recall, 1 on serial 7s, 1 on visuospatial copy, 1 on writing). Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) 19/30. Notably impaired on clock drawing (placed numbers incorrectly, could not set hands to correct time). Difficulty with intersecting pentagons. Unable to accurately copy a cube. Spontaneous speech fluent with occasional word-finding pauses. Serial 7s slow, with one error in five subtractions.

neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch, pinprick, and temperature sensation intact throughout. Proprioception intact at great toes bilaterally. Graphesthesia impaired in both hands (could not identify numbers drawn on palms). Stereognosis mildly impaired bilaterally.
